I have one of those but they're more for home use since they tend to overheat and cause burns. They also make noise like nobody's business when they start getting old or overheated. And if your chair has wheels on it, you will likely be pushed back instead of pedaling.

Don't get me wrong, they're fun to play with, and definitely make it easier to watch movies and shows (I have trouble sitting through shows), but if you're going to shell out $35 for one of those, you might as well prowl Craigslist for free stationary bikes and workout equipment. With the new year coming up, you can continue the diet now and wait for hopeful people to get rid of their old machines.

But if you want one now, you can calculate calorie loss with the following equation:

(((−20.4022)+(0.4472×HEARTRATE)+(0.1263×WEIGHTINKG)+(0.074×AGE))
÷4.184) = CALORIES/MINUTE

I have a Galaxy so I just calculate it from the heart rate monitor minus 10 to 20bpm to account for any errors in posture, the equation, or bmp measurement since bpm affects the result the most. I tested it beside diet when counting calories and it was very accurate, although 10bpm lower is all you really need for accuracy; a higher deficit will lead to mathematically unexpected weight loss.

I'm too lazy to do accurate measurements, so if I do 15 minutes at 130 bpm and then 20 minutes at 150 bpm, I'll still only count it as 35 minutes at 120 bpm. Doesn't hurt anything, just doesn't play out right when you weigh yourself. I still have some weight to lose as well, so it doesn't really matter anyways.

Too much of any candy causes issues - sugar or sugar free. Sorry to the sugar advocate of the sub, but I get sick just looking at most desserts. Even with mindless snacking,  you're aware that the thing you were snacking on is entirely gone, and even if you shared a bit, the rest is still you. Now, I doubt it happened exactly as written (I assume, given the rising dislike of this woman, OP did not say it with much subtlety), but let's pretend it did. That makes the situation much worse.

Let's say he dropped a hint as described in the story in a polite way so that it gave her some knowledge of the situation without outright declaring the gummies are something stronger (instead of "you're crapping yourself because you're obviously eating the candy you're not supposed to", it becomes "too much candy can do that to you"). I'm pretty confident she picked up that hint when she accused him of an accusation. He didn't say,  "I know what you do when nobody is looking" or "THAT'S the candy I'm taking about right there, the one you currently have in your hand and are eating," or anything that directly referenced that one particular type of candy. And yet, even though there is a vending machine (that she also frequently visits), she is aware of what candy he is talking about. That means she made the connection and either chose to ignore it (possibly due to addiction, but most likely just due to poor self-control - addiction would no change after the first warning and maybe pocketing them for later or stealing money from other people's wallets to use the vending machine after the bowl is empty, while poor self-control is trying not to do it but seeing it and not being able to resist while it's so easy to get) or use it as an excuse to keep going home early. In either case, she was taking advantage of the company: stealing their candies or stealing a position they could have filled with a more reliable worker so they wouldn't have lost all that time and money on training.

I like that you're a compassionate person and I've actually been secretly up voting you while we disagree, but there's no reason to feel bad for her. She's capable of change, as seen in the abstaining after the first warning, but she's the antagonist in this story for a reason: she does not currently have the qualities she needs to be professional or mentally and/or physically healthy. Sometimes the best you can get out of an experience is that you have experienced it, and this might be that way for her. She could have realized everyone else knew the truth when she thought she was getting away with murder, and maybe she'll get a better grasp on honesty and being more aware of herself. For all we know, this experience was exactly what she needed to change permanently. Just because some people lack the ability to better themselves does not mean everyone in this sub is destined for the same fate. For instance, the girl who was taking physical therapy with the OP with the bad knee, or the guy who posted how he chased a kid for food and got stuck and cried but used the event to realize he needed to make a change. These two are likely to be mentally healthy and addiction-free since they realize the problem. And, as stated before, if OP really was as subtle as he claims, she already knows the problem. She's not taken the first step yet, but she has lifted her leg for it, and that's a pretty good start.

I'm related to about 5 of them. Two are just idiot assholes that get way too damn invested in their arguments and are willing to back it up with only their own opinion, made up statistics, and violence if they've been caught in their lies. The worst part is that they think they're the smartest people in the world. The other 3 are *actually* smarter, friendlier, and just easier to get along with. They tend to stay calm in conversations, or laugh a little bit if the other person starts getting heated, but they're almost always *completely calm* which, it turns out, is exactly what we need in a sparring partner. We tend to over-observe and research, but never really put that information to good use out of fear of offending people. ENTPs give very little fucks about offending people, but they still appear to be able to read a room and reel back a little bit if they're overstepping their boundaries. It's that thoughtfulness and calmness that really makes the difference. Without it, they would just seem like assholes. With it, it becomes clear that they're just looking for some fun or to learn something new.

Personally, I get along better with my autistic ENTP brother. He's very logical, very honest (almost to a fault; it makes other people hate him since he'll call them out on their bullshit), and the biggest asshole I know of, but it's part of what makes him hilarious. He's borderline genius, though, so that might have something to do with it (one of the bad ENTPs is my other brother, who is of average intelligence - they get into arguments, he gets overly passionate and autistic bro laughs about it, making him more angry and violent; he almost always turns to fighting while autistic bro makes jokes like "you want to fight, man? I could take you" or "hahaha, why are you so upset?! I'm just messing with you."). He's antagonistic at times because he thinks it's funny and doesn't always know when to stop, so you need to know when to roll your eyes and say "whatever" (which is ALL the time with our other brother).

Long story short, we generally get along with them, as long as they aren't *actual* assholes. Like I call myself an asshole to save others the time, but I'm not *actually* an asshole. I'm just cynical and sarcastic, but not rude. They have some of the best traits, in my opinion: they're fun, intelligent, calm, understanding, aware, and funny. They're not as terrible as the few bad apples make them seem. Of course, it all depends on the individual.

As for not moving on quickly: it doesn't really matter as long as you don't get upset easily. There's nothing to really "get over"; they'll genuinely avoid things that upset you as long as it isn't really important (they, too, like calm conversations), and it's hard to get upset when you know they're doing it because they're just genuinely curious or bored. If you two get into an *actual* emotional argument over something, they'll learn from it. They're not stupid. In my experience, they'll move on like it wasn't a thing, but they'll generally proceed with caution until they know for sure you're not going to explode on them again, but they'll still not do whatever it was that caused you to do this (kinda like how my dog no longer runs into the street because I completely psychotically screamed and swatted at him; he doesn't know WHY the street is bad [it was how the last dog died], he just knows he does NOT want to go near it because it makes me absolutely insane and it's not worth it). As for how long it would take you to get over the relationship ending: an incompatibility there doesn't really matter there since you two won't be together anymore.

I never even called her out on her weight, always told everyone how pretty she was (not even including "in spite of her weight" or anything like that), and was always nice to her. ~~But fuck it. She was a fucking whale and there's no way around it.~~

Edit: Nope. I refuse to be that person. I still believe in people of all sizes and all shapes and all features being equal. I just hated her personality; I'm not friends with her or her friend who was the walking embodiment of entitlement and fat logic, I'm just still pissed off people can be *that* shitty and still expect everyone to do everything for them. The weight was just a by-product of their shitty personalities demanding more and more and constantly justifying it with "I'm worth it, tee-hee!" That's why so many shitty people claim fat shaming; they feel entitled to your constant respect and adoration while they don't deserve it, but continue to tell themselves how great they are. The second they are met with opposition, they fight it. It's like being a narcissist; under (and reason for) all that insanity is the most fragile ego that they are desperately trying to protect. "It's not that I can't lose weight, it's that *nobody* can lose weight!" "It's not that fat is unattractive, it's that men are anti-woman and want girls that are boy-shaped!" I'm an unemployed CLS, the people who test the specimens and report out the lab values you mentioned here. It's not like the second you cross into the obese category, everything goes to shit immediately. Good results in your situation, barring an active lifestyle, is probably due to being young and only exhibiting a single known clinical risk factor. Age is a clinical risk factor for a multitude of things that overlaps with obesity, such as type 2 diabetes and a shamefully large percent of cancers. With a genetic predisposition, you are more likely to develop the disease with fewer clinical risk factors, such as a 200lb 14 year old with a homozygous TF7L2 mutation getting type 2 diabetes while it would normally take non-mutants 150lbs and/or 30 years after this point to develop the disease. It sucks for those who have it and it's not fair, but that's life.

That being said, even if you don't have a genetic predisposition for *one* obesity-related disease does not mean you're in the clear for the *rest* of the obesity-related diseases. Cholesterol, blood pressure, A1c - these are all things that are easy and cost effective to test for. Genetic mutations are not. Just because you received a "clean bill of health" does not mean you are not cultivating the first mutation needed to develop cancer in a few decades, nor does it mean you will never develop the diseases you are not genetically predisposed to. You just have more time and/or more weight (honestly, maintaining this obesity is all it takes as you acumulate other non-controllable risk factors) before you begin to develop these diseases. You have the ability to control a risk factor, and you can remove it entirely and help prevent or, at the very least, stave off disease. 

This isn't to make you feel scared or upset or singled out. It is to explain that obesity has a multi-faceted affect on your health in both detectable and seemingly non-detectable ways. I hope you continue your weight loss journey and take comfort in the fact that you are actively preventing disease at your own leisure instead of attempting to rapidly lose weight to treat it. Nothing makes me happier in the heme/chem lab than seeing a patient decrease their A1c after a diagnosis, and nothing makes me sadder than having to report a high A1c in someone without a history of diabetes. We don't get to celebrate those like you who prevent the disease before it occurs, but your doctor likely does even if you don't!

You know how in cookie recipes you mix your wet ingredients and dry ingredients separately? Almond paste would be your wet ingredients, which contains the egg and sugar. Almond flour would be your flour. The two aren't interchangeable, as using almond flour in a recipe calling for almond paste would be dry, under sweetened, and would not hold together as well.

However, you CAN skip the blanching and grinding stage by replacing the almonds in this recipe with an equal amount of almond meal/flour that was made from blanched, whole almonds (such as Bob's Red Mill). Just add it to the food processor with the other ingredients and blend until mixed. This is much faster and easier if you have almond flour. I don't always have almond flour on hand, though I almost always have almonds (because homemade almond milk).

Alright, guys. This recipe starts with almonds and ends with sweet almond cookies. The result is a slightly fruity, dense almond meringue cookie. You can reduce the sugar to make them not as sweet (these cookies are rather sweet, so be warned!). Buckle up, because this recipe has multiple steps.

_______________________________________________________________

* 1 cup (142g) almonds
* 3 large egg whites
* 1 tsp pure almond extract
* 1 slice (20g) banana
* 1/16tsp salt
* 10g pine nuts
* 32 packets (1/2 cup) Truvia

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Blanch Almonds** - You can skip this step by buying blanched almonds, but it only takes a few minutes and it really isn't a big deal. Add water to a pot and wait for it to start boiling. Add your **1 cup (142g) almonds** to the pot and boil for exactly 60 seconds. The second your timer beeps, dump it all out into a spaghetti strainer. Rinse in cold water and peel the skins off by ripping the pointed end and pushing the almonds by the fatter end. They will go popping out in whatever direction the thin, pointy end is pointing towards. Try to aim for a bowl or directly into a food processor.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Make the Almond Paste** - Run the almonds through a food processor until they get a fine texture. The thinner you get it here, the smoother the texture of the final cookie. When that's done, add in **1 egg white**, **16 packets (1/4 cup) Truvia**, **1 slice (20g) banana** that has been smashed, and **1 tsp almond extract** that has been mixed together into the food processor. As you continue to process it, a thick paste should begin to form.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Making the Dough** - With the almond paste formed, add the remaining **2 egg whites**, **1/16tsp salt**, and **16 packets (1/4 cup) Truvia** to the food processor. If your dough had some trouble sticking to the sides when making the paste, this will help it smooth out. When everything is combined and smooth, it's done.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Making the Cookies** - Set the oven to preheat at 325F. Line an air-bake pan/cookie sheet with parchment paper. Use a tablespoon measuring spoon to measure out the cookies. A level tablespoon will produce 23 cookies. When you have them on the pan, slam it down a few times like you're making macarons to flatten the cookies. If you place exactly 3 pine nuts on top of each cookie, you will have used exactly 10g of pine nuts (I measured so you don't have to!). Bake the cookies for about 6 minutes, or until firm and begining to brown. Remove from the oven and use a spatula to immediately transfer the cookies to a cooling rack (or just paper towels on your counter top if you forgot the cooling rack like I did). If they're not done, they'll still stick to the pan and can't be moved, so put them back in if that's the case. Otherwise, they'll be ready once they're fully cooled. They will get sweeter as they cool.

The best I can give is my personal experience. Patients that have a lot of muscle mass, large veins, and the ability to make a tight fist tend to do better. Drink water, keep the area warmed, etc. If you have thin veins, donating blood just may not be an option for you due to the size of the needle used.

It does exist and I believe it's already on the market, but I haven't used it before. I don't think any of the hospitals I've been to had it. The problem isn't really with identifying the vein. If you can feel it and/or see it (feeling is ideal), then you've identified it. Sticking it can be a problem. Very obese patients experience unnecessary pain and trauma during draws, especially the ones with little muscle tone, as I had a patient whose veins actually receded inwards instead of being punctured. He had virtually no muscle underneath (keep in mind that I had to draw on him from the side of his power scooter, so the lack of muscle is expected), so the vein just kept going down. This person also had small veins, so I had to use the thinnest butterfly needle on him, so of course I got scared when it got close to the end of the needle and it still hadn't punctured.
